title: Isolation, Containment and Trust
results: Isolation, containment, authority reduction, trust and sandbox are distinct concepts.
Isolation is dimension- and threat-model-scoped non-interference rather than a scalar sandbox flag.
Integrity, confidentiality and availability isolation are independent axes.
Isolation is distinct from atomicity, immutability and determinism.
Containment bounds propagation/lifetime/resources while lifecycle containment does not imply containment or undo of external Effects.
Authority attenuation reduces blast radius without automatically creating hostile-code isolation.
Trust is an assumption about actor/component behavior under retained authority and is not an enforcement mechanism.
Current trusted_local is broad owner-trusted installed-service-user authority and is not a hostile-code sandbox.
Workspace reservations, source commitments and Runtime API path scopes are coordination/precondition/policy boundaries rather than per-Workspace kernel isolation.

Current contained_local is a composite partial isolation and authority-reduction profile using private network, capability removal, no-new-privileges, filesystem restrictions, non-root payload identity, environment reduction and narrower cache paths.
Current contained_local correctly rejects kernel-grade hostile-code, multi-tenant, complete-confidentiality, controlled-egress and disposable-machine claims.
Linux namespaces isolate specific resource classes rather than providing universal isolation.
Mount namespaces make path resolution namespace-relative and P4 is both an epistemic and authority/isolation falsifier.
Non-root UID, user namespace, no-new-privileges and capability removal are distinct authority controls.
Read-only and hidden filesystem views constrain specific mount/path channels without implying complete confidentiality.
Environment filtering reduces ambient credential/configuration authority but is not a secret broker.
Immutable input materialization is a strong scoped input-integrity/read-only boundary and not a whole-environment isolation claim.
Read-only guarantees are actor-scoped; root/elevated administrators may remain outside the constrained authority set.
cgroup budgets improve availability isolation while systemd cgroups/process groups and Windows Job Objects primarily provide lifecycle/resource containment.
Killing all owned descendants does not undo information flow or external Effects already emitted.
Windows limited token is authority attenuation and differs materially from AppContainer isolation; elevated token is broader authority rather than stronger isolation.
AppContainer demonstrates default-restricted per-application file/network/process/credential isolation while Windows Sandbox/VM demonstrates a separate-kernel hardware-virtualized boundary.
Namespace/container shared-kernel and VM separate-kernel boundaries have different TCB and failure-domain properties.
Shared caches and persistent state are explicit cross-Job coupling dimensions affecting integrity, confidentiality, availability and later determinism.
Current owner-trusted single-operator Runtime is qualitatively different from mutually hostile multi-tenant execution, which is explicitly unsupported.
Root/elevated supervisor plus non-root payload is privilege separation but remains same-kernel.
Detective controls such as path witnesses improve evidence/recovery but are not preventive isolation boundaries.
Ingress authentication/authorization is separate from realized target isolation.
Strong hostile/disposable execution should normally be delegated to an external isolation owner whose provider/profile identity can be bound into Runtime rather than widening current profile claims.
The governing law is IsolationClaimScope <= EnforcedBoundaryScope.

nextRound.title: Determinism, Nondeterminism and Agent Action
nextRound.entryQuestion: Given explicit inputs, authority and isolation boundaries, which hidden or open state can still make repeated realizations diverge, and what can Runtime truthfully claim about determinism, reproducibility, hermeticity and replay?

notes: RF13 explains current isolation and trust boundaries but does not authorize new sandbox mechanisms, VM/AppContainer integration, per-Job users, controlled egress, secret brokers, hostile multi-tenancy or production API changes.
